It is as fair for one as for the other.

Surely, as far as that is concerned. At the same time, if they have to travel any distance, I think it would be only .fair to pay their expenses. I only put this forward as a suggestion to the minister, because I think he wants to do what is reasonable and right in the matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
As I have already
stated, this provision, as well as. the preceding one, are reproduced from the existing Soldiers' Voting Act. With regard to
[The Chairman.]
the suggestion that we should pay the expenses of deputy scrutineers, their number is left entirely in the discretion of the party which is to he represented, just as on this side of the Atlantic the Candidate determines how many agents or representatives he requires. If we provided for payment of those deputy scrutineers, we could hardly undertake to allow the liberty which I think each party ought to have to provide the number of representatives it requires. On this side of the Atlantic the parties provide their representatives, and there has never been a suggestion that the people of the country should pay for them. The suggestion now made is that persons who are there purely as representatives of political parties should be paid, by the general public. I must confess this hardly commends .itself to my judgment. It would certainly be a new departure. Both parties at every camp and every place where there will be voting will have their adherents. No. one suggests that in any camp there will not be many Liberals as well as many Conservatives. The deputy scrutineer at a particular camp would in all probability be a man appointed from that camp, so that if the parties act reasonably in providing their representatives there will be very small expenses involved. In any event, the function of these officers is purely and simply to be party representatives, and in all our past history I do' not know of a case where the public authority has been asked to pay the expenses of purely party representatives.
'Mr. NESBITT:	As ia matter of fact the
candidate pays it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It is paid by the candidate, or the party, or whoever the funds may come from. In any event, it is not paid by the Government of the country, that is, by the people generally. This is another instance in which we are merely following what is >a general and well-established practice and custom, and to pass a law providing for the payment of the expenses of such an indefinite number of party representatives might entail upon the country an expense which certainly I am not in a position to foresee at the present time. Aside from that, it would be a new departure in principle if we should provide for the payment of the travelling expenses of party representatives. It may be suggested that we have departed from the principle to the extent of the six scrutineers 'who are to be jointly appointed. But at the time Parliament passed the existing legislation, that

action was thought justifiable under the circumstances, so that if it were considered necessary or desirable by either or both parties to send three representatives from this country to take charge from the party point of view of the conduct of the election, that they at all events would be enabled to go over there and have their expenses paid. Then it was put into their hands to provide all the deputy scrutineers they thought proper for their respective parties in the manner they thought most effective and best. I do not remember that at the time this legislation was adopted it was urged that we ought to pay the expenses of those party representatives.

I think a moment's reflection will show that subsection' 2 ie closely related to paragraph (d). I do' not see how we can fairly dispose of the former until we know what disposition is to be made of the latter. If those presiding officers as provided for by paragraph (d) are to be non-partisan, selected by the leader of the Government,and the leader of the Opposition, then there is not the eame necessity for scrutineers, because they will be careful to have the deputy presiding officers also non-partisan in character and fairly representative of both sides. I submit to the committee, however, that if the minister should insist that we are not to consider paragraph (d) open for amendment, and that the right to have partisan presiding officers should be retained, then the Liberal party should not be compelled to pay the expenses of deputy scrutineers to go around to the various camps in England and in France and see that those partisan deputy presiding officers do their duty. I do not think that would be reasonable, and that is why I respectfully submitted my suggestion to the minister, not imagining for a moment that I would arouse his ire, that subsection 2 and paragraph (d) of subsection 1 should be considered together. The minister says that under no circumstances should those deputy scrutineers be paid. It is all very well for the minister to say that, when he has the appointment of the men who are to carry on the elections, who are to control the elections, who are to take the vote, and who may go around, as provided for by the other dispositions of the Bill, in charge of the ballots. It is all very well for the minister to say the Government party will pay their own scrutineers, hut our position is different. If subsection (d) passes in the language in which if is at present drawn, we would have no voice in the appointment of
those deputy presiding officers. They would be appointed by and in the interests of the Government party. However, if the minister insists upon subsection 2 being considered now, without waiting to dispose of paragraph (d), of course there is nothing for me to do but interpose my objection to it.
It has not been made very plain how these votes are to be taken. We have been told how the vote shall be counted, that the ballots are to be put into this bag, but I submit to the committee that the important thing is that the votes shall be properly put into that receptacle. So far all I have been able to learn about these officers, whose pay we are providing foT, is that somebody will go round the country with a receptacle into which he is permitted to put votes. We are told that we may have scrutineers. I have no idea how many of these men will be engaged in taking the vote or at how many places those votes will be taken at the same time. Will there be any particular number of those places at which votes will be received? How many scrutineers will a man naturally need to have in order to be represented at these polls? It is absolutely impossible to apply the machinery of an election in Canada to the branch of the election which is to be conducted as provided for in the Bill. It is no use to attempt to apply that machinery whilch is made for the ordinary home election to an election taken in France, ot Great Britain. The minister says to us: " You can appoint your scrutineers at home; why not do the same thing abroad?" When an election is gding on in my own county I know a few people in every polling district. I can trust my friends in each polling district to see that the poll is being properly conducted. A great many of them would not ask any payment for doing it-perhaps none of them would- but here we are told that the same machinery is to be transferred to France, where I do not know anybody, where I have not the faintest idea of how many polls there are going to be and in regard to which this Bill does not help me. The minister says to me: " You fcan appoint a scrutineer." I do not know how many places I will have to arrange for; I do not know who may be taking the vote; but the minister says: ''this is what happens at home and this is what you must do abroad." What ha3 been suggested by my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) is what strikes me as the only fair



and decent way to everybody; that is to appoint a non-partisan commission. Let them all meet together, and go around together and take these votes.
Then there should be confidence and an opportunity of avoiding those horrors which happened in the British Columbia election. As to asking us to pay for the scrutineers and giving us an opportunity of doing so, I regard it as absolutely impossible for myself to be represented in England, France, Belgium, Scotland and all those places where a soldier may be found and in which I have not the faintest idea where a poll will be held. If I had the money of a Vanderbilt, and was able to pay all the men whose employment is suggested under this Bill, I cannot see how the thing could be done. The whole thing, as the Prime Minister has said, is absolutely impracticable and impossible.

With respect to clause 2, it has occurred to me that the Minister of Justice has got into trouble because he has been too fair. It is difficult for me to conceive of anything that is fairer than this clause. Hon. gentlemen complain that scrutineers are not paid. Paragraph 2 says:
Such officers and functionaries and their deputies, clerks and assistants, except scrutineers and deputy scrutineers, may be paid and reimbursed as the Governor General in Council may provide, authorize or allow; scrutineers may be paid,, their actual travelling: and living expenses only, at a rate to be fixed by the Governor Genera] in Council; deputy scrutineers shall not be paid or reimbursed out of the fund of Canada any sums whatever.
The functionaries mentioned in that section are to be paid.
Who are they?
Such officers and functionaries, and their deputies, clerks and assistants, as are taking the election, except scrutineers and deputy scrutineers-
All appointed by the Government.

Never mind by whom they are appointed; we will come to the question of partisanship later on. They are to be reimbursed as the Governor in Council may provide, authorize or allow. Scrutineers may get their actual travelling and living expenses. Outside of this second paragraph, there is a paragraph referring to scrutineers and deputy scrutineers. Who are they? If you will refer to subsection (e) you will see that it provides that:
Any scrutineer may, by writing, appoint any necessary deputies-

Any necessary deputies. The hon. member for Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) says: We do not know how many there will be. There will be as many as may be necessary and each party shall name its own particular scrutineers. There are allowed to the Liberal party under this Act three scrutineers and they can appoint as many deputies as they like and they can send them where they please. The Conservatives can do the same thing for the conduct of the election. There is absolute fairness between the parties. The minister has gone further in this Act than any minister has ever been known to go in the history of partisan politics in Canada when he has given to the Opposition the right to appoint scrutineers to represent thetn, to preside over the election and to count the ballots. To my mind the hon. gentlemen opposite are unfair in their criticism. The Minister of Justice has brought it on himself because of his extra fairness in departing from what has been from time immemorial held as a Government prerogative that governments conduct the elections by their own officers appointed by themselves. The moment that this Government gives a concession to hon. gentlemen opposite, we have the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) talking, and talking, and talking by the hour over a clause which he was told was to be allowed to stand.
Not by the hour.

Yes, really by the hour. Although the clause had been allowed to stand the hon. gentleman talked persistently and travelled entirely abroad from the clause, apparently approaching pretty close to the idea of obstruction. Is the hon. gentleman wishing to cast an aspersion on the ability or intentions of their own scrutineers? Does he mean to cast an aspersion on the conduct of this election by the men whom his leader will appoint? Can he not trust anybody? Can the hon. gentleman not trust men appointed by his own leader? What is the matter? What has gone wrong with the mental attitude of hon. gentlemen opposite who are imbued and thoroughly soused with suspicion about what is one of the fairest clauses ever put upon the statute book, giving hon. gentlemen a chance of preventing unfairness, giving them the right to name officials contrary to the past practice, applying the principle of fifty-fifty, three Liberal scrutineers to three Conservative scrutineers and giving them every facility to see that the election is conducted honestly, and yet the suspicion is still

there, still engendered in the individual minds of, I am thankful to say, a few only of the hon. gentlemen opposite.
Perhaps the hon. gentleman would tell me at how many places and by bow many officers .the vote will be taken on the same day.
It is not for .me to say that. I suppose that is all worked out in the Bill.
What is the good of having these six scrutineers when we may have thirty places at which votes are being taken?
Deputies could be sent there.

If hon. gentlemen would think a little .about the conditions they would not see so many difficulties about the deputy scrutineers. Deputy scrutineers would be soldiers residing and on duty at the place where the ballot was to be taken. They would have no travelling to do in ordinary cases, because a strange soldier would not be nearly as proficient to act as scrutineer as one familiar with all the men stationed at that polling place. Then these men are already under pay as soldiers. Their pay would not be diminished, and if they had to travel, as some hon. gentlemen apprehend, they could only travel by permission of their superior officers. The Government, both in France and England, control the railways and issue transportation to soldiers, who cannot travel except by permission, so that in practice there would be no difficulty about travelling expenses of deputy scrutineers or their living expenses while on duy.	'

May I point out the difficulty. Suppose a vote is being taken at a certain camp in England. There may be dozens of people from my county there of whose whereabouts I do not know, and I should be absolutely helpless in trying to find .some one to represent me.
The hon. gentleman is no worse off than any other member.
I was speaking generally; every one is the same.

Every other hon. member is the same except in this, that the Government appoints the men to carry on this whole business of taking the vote and the country pays for them. The Liberals of this country pay as well as the Conser-
301 i
vatives. We pay all of these returning officers and deputy returning officers.
Not the scrutineers.
You do not need scrutineers if you have deputies. You will be careful, il I know you well, to have the right kind of men as deputy returning officers and as deputy presiding officers.

Good, honest men.
' Mr. PUGSLEY: I have no doubt of that. But unless the minister changes his mind there is to be no voice by the Opposition in the appointing of the presiding officer or the deputy presiding officers. Take myself or the hon. member for Cape Breton as an example. What do I know about selecting a deputy scrutineer in France? Will the commanding officers allow the. soldiers to act as deputy scrutineers? I doubt very much if they will. They have other duties to perform and it will simply mean-	.
Perhaps they would not let them vote because they have military duties.
That is different. They might let them vote but might hesitate about letting them perform political work in the way of representing a political party.

It is quite impossible in most cases, especially in France, to have other than military scrutineers, as civilians would not be allowed to go to the lines where it would be necessary to hold most of the polls.

The minister is proposing an election which would be similar to an election held in Canada without the opportunity for people to be represented at the polling places, and I submit again that the only way to do that is by a commission.

I think the proposal isa reasonable one and that the minister-should consider whether the deputy scrutineers should be paid their travelling expenses. It has been pointed out that tue Government appoints the returning officers ai;d they will naturally be friends of the Government. They will be men in whom the Government have every confidence, and they will feel that the election will be held fairly, as far as they are concerned, by the officers whom they appoint. The only officer who will represent the Opposition at the poll will be the deputy scrutineer. There are six scrutineers, but I presume these six will be reserved for the counting of the ballots after the election is over and that

it is not pretended that these six scrutineers who are appointed and whose expenses will be paid can he present at the various polls where the election is held. Consequently there is no- way in which the Opposition can be represented at the different polls excepting by the deputy scrutineers, and as the officers who take the poll are Government officers, appointed by the Government and paid by the Government out of the funds of the country, is it not fair to consider whether the deputy scrutineers should not also be paid? I think it is. I think it is a proposition the minister ought to consider. I have no doubt that the Minister of Justice desires to give us a fair ballot and that there should-be fair play on both sides. We all know it would not be likely to be a fair election unless both sides were represented at every poll where ballots were taken.
Did the hon. member say both sides?
I did.
I thought there was only one side now.

Then they have all
pome to the Liberal side?

I should say that officers should be present to represent the [DOT]Opposition in every poll where votes are taken, otherwise you cannot expect to have a result in which the people will have confidence. It is not like an election in Canada, where a man has his friends in every polling district, who take an interest in his election. That we all know is the practice in Canada. But it is a very different thing when we are carrying on an election in a foreign country among men scattered in various places, none of us knowing where they are and it being impossible for us to be fully represented. Consequently the circumstances are so entirely different that I think the minister ought to take that question into his consideration.

Is the hon. member
contending that the Opposition should have the privilege of sending men from Canada to England or France to act as scrutineers in the interest of the Opposition?

No, I would not suggest that it would be advisable to do that. I do not think that could be done. I have no doubt that men on the other side, soldiers or civilians, will be selected who will have leisure to attend to these matters. It would be very expensive indeed to send

men across the ocean, and I do not think that would be practicable. But there may be some expense in connection with travelling and attending to places where the vote is taken, and I think that that would be a legitimate expense for this country to bear.
The language of the section is rather peculiar. It says: " the deputy scrutineers shall not be paid or reimbursed out of the fund of Canada." I do not know any money that is described as the fund of Canada. I have heard of consolidated revenue, but I do not think this is the ordinary legal language. The impression given by this section is that there is a fund somewhere that is not the fund of Canada on which one side, at all events, professes to draw in order to pay its officers. I suppose that is the inference; it is a fund but not a fund of Canada.

The hon. gentleman from North Perth should not complain about hon. members on this side of the House discussing this question, in view of the statement of the Prime Minister that one of the questions which occasioned the Government a great deal of care and worry for a long period was in regard to the soldiers' vote, as is referred to in the correspondence with the ex-Minister of Public Works, when the Prime Minister pointed out that the Government had spent a long time in preparing this Bill and bringing it to Parliament, with tremendous detail. I think the hon. member should withdraw the suggestion that we are discussing this Bill unduly. Voting is to take place in France and England, and hon. gentlemen say there is no use in arranging for civilian scrutineers, as the scrutineers must be in military service. Where is the provision that, if a man wants a vote taken in a particular camp, he is to have the right to go there, and that transportation will be given to him? My hon. friend from Cape Breton might discover some friend over there whom he would like to have appointed scrutineer in a certain district. This man may come along and get his rations, but he is not going to get any money for his trip. The Government has the lists of all the men overseas, and hon. gentlemen on this side of the House are not in the same position in that respect. How are people to know, when engaged in a contest in a county here, whether the interest of particular candidates over there are being looked after?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Our three men from the Opposition will nominate the scrutineers.

These men are not going to be omniscient. Suppose the hon. gentleman from Cape Breton has a battalion in a particular place, and desires to appoint some friend to be deputy scrutineer, to see that the vote is properly taken, how would it be worked out? Apparently the voting is taking place simultaneously all over; the soldiers are not going to vote in one camp one day and in another camp another day.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The hon. gentleman from Cape Breton would have nothing to say about it. The three men nominated over there would have the say.

But they do not know everybody from Vancouver to Sydney, and the only way they could know would be by my hon. friend from Cape Breton, or some one else, writing them and saying he would like to have a certain man appointed scrutineer.
Every member is in the same position.
I know that. How is the man he might want to have appointed scrutineer to get his expenses? I should like to have that question answered.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think I have explained several times that this is the section that exists in the Soldiers' Vote Act, and the question was all threshed out when that Act was passed, and this is an entirely novel suggestion that the people of Canada should be called upon to pay party representatives. The hon. gentleman asks: where are we going to get the transportation for the gentleman the hon. member for Cape Breton will select as scrutineer, and who will have to travel from place to place? If an election ie being held in Montreal and I determine I would like to have a man from Vancouver to act as my scrutineer, I do not know what reception I would get in the House, if I came and said the people of the country should pay the expense of that gentleman from Vancouver. I must confess I have difficulty in following the reasoning that suggests that the expenses of party representatives on each side should be paid by the people of Canada. The hon. gentleman is discussing this question as though the hon. member for Cape Breton was going to select his personal friend to be scrutineer for him. If hon. gentlemen look at the Bill they will see we are not undertaking any gigantic scheme to provide scrutineers for individual candidates. If any hon. gentleman thinks he can afford that luxury, we will not prevent him, but we are following the method which met the approval of this House when the Soldiers' Vote Bill was passed. That leaves it open to the party to provide themselves with such representatives as they desire. We give them absolute liberty in that regard, and recognize all the representatives and give them machinery to provide for representatives, but we feel that, when we have done that, we can hardly be called upon to go further, andy pay the expenses of these representatives.
Just as candidates in Canada find scrutineers available at .the places where they are required, I should think the representatives of the respective parties would be able to find persons at the different places where polls are going to be held whom they could appoint as deputy scrutineers. It was not really incumbent upon Parliament to make this legislation to provide for party representation at all, but we have done it because it seemed to us a fair thing to do, under the circumstances. To suggest that it .should be pushed further, and that we should impose upon the people of Canada the expense that properly belongs to the respective parties is a suggestion which it is quite imposible for me to accept.

No person, so far as I know, is looking for any charity from the Minister of Justice in regard to any legitimate election expense that the candidate should bear, but we are looking for an opportunity for proper representation of each party at every place where the poll is to be taken. Let the minister form a camimis-sion under this Bill; let the Government appoint some competent man .as chairman, with whose appointment we will have nothing to do. Let an equal number of men be selected on each side, and let the Opposition pay their share of the expense, and the Conservatives pay theirs. Then the commission could report, and could assure us that every vote .was taken.
Then we shall know that things will be o'one in a proper and honest way. Under this provision certain persons have the right to travel around the country trailing bags after them, with the opportunity of piling into those bags the ballots of men that they meet on the streets. Yet I am told that we have nothing to complain of. The hon. minister says: a scrutineer will be appointed; we will not pay him; you can pay him if you like. Is that a satisfactory answer to the suggestion that these officials will be trailing bags around with them and filling them up with paper; that the fate-

of the people so far as government during the next five years is concerned will depend upon what those officials put in those bags? That is what I complain about. The provision is not fair; it is absolutely partisan; it is capable of producing absolutely scandalous results. We have evidence from British Columbia that on a non-partisan question-that of whether liquor shall be sold in British Columbia or not-corruption of the worst kind developed; there was double and treble voting; rascality in its worst form was perpetrated. If these things happened in such a case as that, what will happen in this case, during the full force and agitation of a Dominion election? We have reason to suppose that under this law conditions will be a thousand times worse than those that prevailed in British Columbia. I have to run my election in Cape Breton county and so far as the vote of the soldiers is concerned I shall be absolutely unrepresented. The minister says that if he should want a scrutineer to look after his poll in Ste. Anne division, he himself would have to pay for that man's services. That is no answer; that does not touch the point at all.

As thejion. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) said, this is not a matter that affects any particular member. It affects every member of the House; it may affect each member in the same way.
I have listened to the discussion during most of the afternoon, .and I have not heard any reason why the number of deputy scrutineers who may be appointed by the scrutineers is unlimited, I assume from what the minister said that the deputy scrutineer will correspond to the scrutineer who acts inside the polling booth during an election in Canada. If that be the fact, I should like to know why an unlimited number of these scrutineers may be appointed. I should also like to have an explanation from the .minister with regard to the expression referred to by the member for Guys borough (Mr. Sinclair): "the fund of Canada ".

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: To answer the last question first, I think that probably the letter " s " has been left out; it being intended that the word " .funds '' should be used as designating the moneys of Canada. It is not intended to convey any other sense than that no money of Canada shall be paid to these people.
Then it should not pass in that way.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I will have that corrected. As to why we allow an indefinite number of scrutineers, it is not possible for us to anticipate how many .scrutineers each party may require in order to provide themselves with .representatives at the polls and at all the different operations of counting *that will be carried on. We therefore leave it to each party-each party being represented by its three scrutineers-to name the deputy scrutineers. The reason why we do not limit the number of deputy scrutineers to be appointed i% in order that each party may be able to provide whatever number it deems necessary. It is prescribed how many representatives each party may have at a particular operation, such .as the taking of the vote. We are now dealing with how many people may be empowered under this Act to act as representatives or agents. We leave it to the discretion of each party as to how many they may require. I do not see that we could definitely prescribe the number. One party may think they need more than another; neither party is in a position to determine at the present moment how many persons they may require as agents. That will depend upon the number of polls that may be held. The intention is to provide as many polls as may be needed to enable us to offer opportunity to all the soldiers to vote. Just in proportion as the voters may be more or less scattered, you will have to have a greater or less number of polls. It is impossible, therefore, to define how many occasions there may be for a party needing the services of a representative. When we come to the particular operation, of course each party is entitled to .a definite number who dhall be present, say, at the taking of the vote. At the taking of a poll each party is entitled to have one representative, but where a number of polls are held at the same time a party may need large numbers of representatives, if it is to be represented at all, at each of the polls. That is why we left this mater to the discretion of the respective parties.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess.
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.
Mr. MURPH1 : When the House rose for dinner the .minister had just explained the reason for not limiting the number of deputy scrutineers to be appointed, and the probable disposal of them in case of an elec-

tion. Did I understand him to say that there was some provision in this Bill similar to that in the Dominion Elections Act, which prohibits more than two agents for each candidate from being in the polling booth at the same time as an elector?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes, the provision will be found in subsection 4 of section 8, which provides that:
The deputy presiding officer shall permit any scrutineer or deputy scrutineer, or, in the absence of both, any one military elector, to be present at any poll, and to act thereat as agent on behalf of any party, with the powers of an agent of a candidate at a poll held under Part III.
The only difference between this provision and the similar provision in the Dominion Elections Act is that we are imposing on the deputy presiding officer the obligation of permitting one scrutineer on behalf of each party rather than two. We cannot, of course, provide for representatives of the individual candidates, or we might have to have 468 scrutineers at each taking of votes.
Subsection agreed to on division.
On subsection 4, section 4-Before whom sworn:

I observe that some of these officers may be sworn before a regimental or battalion commanding officer. Is there any authority empowering a regimental or battalion commanding officer to administer oaths other than that contained in this Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The only other provision that I know of for their -administering the oath is when the soldiers attest. The Military Voters' Act of 1915 confers this power upon the officers.

I would suggest that the minister add, after the word " officer," in line 6, the words " or officer in charge of an independent unit." I have 'in mind certain cases where large bodies of our troops in France are not in charge of a regimental or battalion commanding officer. For instance, the three Canadian tunnelling companies who are now -at Y-pres, and have been there for the last year and a half, are under the command of a captain or major. They are called independent companies and number about 800 to a company, the three companies comprising in round figures about 2,500 men. There are other cases of this kind where isolated bodies of Canadian troops in France are not in charge of a regimental or battalion commanding
officer-in connection with the divisional trains, for instance.

Would the suggested
amendment of my hon. friend be wide enough to cover cases similar to the ones he has cited, though perhaps not exactly analogous?
I think so.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: While I am willing to accept the suggestion, we are dealing here only with oaths to be taken by officers under this Act, not with oaths to be taken by the individual soldier who comes to vote. Most of these captains would probably be able to find some other officer who was empowered to administer the oath. But I am quite willing to accept the suggestion, as it might be useful.
Is the form of oath to be taken by these different officials included in the Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No form is provided. The provision is that they shall be sworn to the faithful performance of their duties. It did not appear to be necessary to make a special form.
I am not so particular about the form. But what record will remain as evidence that the oath was administered and taken? There should be something of that kind among the papers.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not think it is necessary for us to specially prescribe here that a record shall be made of the taking of the oath. This whole provision is to form part of the Dominion Elections Act. We are prescribing for those things which are to be done differently from the procedure under the General Elections Act, and what we -are providing here to be differently done is as to the persons before whom the oaths may be taken. I am rather under the impression that the form with regard to these oaths under the general law, whatever it is, would apply here, but I will look into the matter and make sure.
The record of these oaths is usually returned in an envelope with the ballot box.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
Do the deputy scrutineers have to be sworn?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
They would require to be sworn if they took any part in an open vote, just -as scrutineers have to be sworn under our present law, if I remember

rightly, when a man has his ballot marked for him. But for the ordinary performance of his duties, the scrutineer is not an official acting on representative public authority in any way, and there is no provision requiring him to take the oath merely because he is a scrutineer.
He takes the oath of secrecy?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, in cases where he is called upon to be present when a voter marks his ballot.

He takes oath at the
beginning of the poll, and that applies to the whole day?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I will look into it. If the general Act requires it, of course it will be followed.

Would the general Act
apply in this case?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There is no provision that this part is to be read as forming part of the general Dominion Elections Act. It is really made part 4 of that Act. We make exceptional provL.ons in this part. As I understand it, the rest would apply where applicable.
Subsection as amended agreed to.
Why not take up paragraphs (c) and (d) of section 4?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Before we take them up,
I might point out that I was asked to let them stand, because it was suggested that the right hon. the leader of the Opposition would probably desire to say something upon them. As he is not present now. would it not be as well to let these paragraphs stand and take up some of the other sections, because we will probably have to come back to theee sections when he is present.

The leader of the Opposition told me he was unable to be present to-night, and he authorized me to state his view to the committee. As the minister seems anxious to get along, I would not like to have these paragraphs delayed, and it is not the desire of the leader of the Opposition that there should be any delay. He stated to me that he regards it as extremely unfair that he should be given the right to name a certain number of the inferior officers, who really have no control whatever over the election, and in regard to the presiding officers, who take the places of the returning officers where the election 
is held in Canada under the ordinary provisions of the Dominion Elections Act, he should have no voice whatever, and that the Government should have the whole right of appointment, thus making them partisan officials. He thinks there should be in paragraph (d) exactly the same provisions as are contained in paragraph (c). Therefore, in order to make them conform, I move in amendment, seconded by Mr. Lemieux:
That paragraph (d) of subsection (1) of section 4 be amended by inserting the word "even" after the word "sufficient" in line 1 of the paragraph, and by inserting after the word "electors" in line 17 the words "half of the number of such presiding officers shall be nominated by the Prime Minister and the other half by the leader of the Opposition."
If I have the permission of our genial friends who occupy seats behind the treasury benches, I would like to make a few remarks in respect of this amendment.
The hon. gentleman recognizes his masters.

I submit this is an
eminently fair and proper amendment, and if it is not accepted it will afford to the people of this country conclusive evidence that this Bill has been so designed as to permit fraud and irregularities in the taking of the soldiers votes. That is the conclusion which inevitably will be drawn from the course of the Government in respect of the Bill. The Bill provides now that the Prime Minister and the leader of the Opposition shall have the right to nominate an equal number of special returning officers, also that the leader of the Opposition shall be allowed to nominate three scrutineers to act jointly with the scrutineers nominated by the Prime Minister. The reason for making that provision is because it is recognized that the soldiers' vote is to be taken under most exceptional and extraordinary circumstances. It is recognized that there are a large number of votes to be taken, and that it is desirable there should be some provision made in the way of safeguards to prevent unfairness. In the case of an election being held in Canada under ordinary circumstances, no such provision would be deemed to be necessary, and no such provision has been made. But, admitting it is necessary to create safeguards along those lines, I would ask you if it is fair simply to allow the leader of the Opposition to have a voice in the naming of the inferior officials, of the men who have no real control in connection with the

holding of the polls and the taking of the votes, and to decline to give him that right and privilege in respect of the higher officers who have all to do with the taking of the vote, with the holding of the polls, and who should exercise absolute fairness and impartiality in order to assure a fair and honest election.
The greatest possible opportunities are necessarily afforded by this Bill for fraud and irregularities. My hon. friend from Pic-tou (Mr. Macdonald) cited instances of gross fraud and irregularities in the taking of the votes of soldiers from British Columbia at the front in respect to a question which was not in any sense of a partisan character. If that were likely to occur in that case, how much more likely is it to occur in this case where there are partisan deputy presiding officers and where there will necessarily be, as there always is in elections, a partisan spirit and a desire on the part of those to whom is entrusted the machinery of the election to win the election for the party with which their sympathies are and the party which has appointed them to discharge this duty. We might avoid that to a very great extent if the presiding officers were appointed jointly upon the nomination of the Prime Minister and the leader of the Opposition. I can see no reason why the Government should allow this in the case of the inferior officers and refuse it in the case of those who are really the important officers and upon whose impartiality and fairness rests the proper conduct of the election. 1 am authorized by the leader of the Opposition, upon whom is imposed by clauses (c) and (e) the duty of joining in the choice of the inferior officers, to state that he considers this Bill will fall far short of giving a fair and reasonable opportunity for an honest and impartial election if the same right is not conferred upon him under clause (d) to join in the appointment of the presiding officers.
The Bill gives very wide powers to these presiding officers, particularly to the deputies who are appointed by the presiding officers. They have very great powers. They are allowed to exercise a wide discretion and in many cases, if they see fit to do so, they may take the votes without any notice whatever to the scrutineers and without the candidates of either political party having any opportunity to say a single word in regard to it. I do appeal to the Minister of Justice, if he cannot accept the suggestion of my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) that there should be a nonpartisan commission to attend to the whole matter, to accept the suggestion and act
upon the request conveyed through me now by the leader of the Opposition, who is not able to be present to-night, that the same provision be inserted in clause (d) with respect to the appointment of the presiding officers, as the minister has inserted in clauses (c) and (e) with respect to the special returning officers and scrutineers.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I understand that the hon. gentleman is moving in amendment that clause (d) should be made to correspond, in so far as the nominations are concerned with clause (c) and that we may take it that (c) is not objected to. I would like to get at it in a regular way so that we could take up the discussion of the amendment to (d) and therefore I would suggest that we dispose of clause (c) first.
I would think that the three clauses ought to go together.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not quite see what we gain by allowing clause (c) to stand while we are dealing with (d) and moving to amend it by applying the principle of
(c)	to (d). Unless it is assumed that the principle that underlies (c) is approved, why should we be seeking to add it to
(d) ?	.

While the leader of the Opposition might be fairly called upon to perform the duty of taking part in the nomination of presiding officers, special returning officers and scrutineers, a duty which he is quite willing to perform, I think it an outrage-and I think I can speak for him when I say it is an outrage -that he should be called upon to perform that duty with respect to the minor officers and should be refused the privilege of performing the same duty in respect to the higher officers.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Am I to understand that if the amendment to (d) were not carried then clause (c) would be looked upon as an outrage to the leader of the Opposition? As 1 understand that the reason why we cannot deal with clause (c) by itself is that if we do not amend clause (d) then clause (c) stands as an outrage to the leader of the Opposition? I have heard many observations during the course of this discussion that have surprised me, but I confess that none has surprised me more than the suggestion that it is an outrage to the leader of the Opposition to confer upon him this right which is conferred by clause (c). I can grasp the complaint, although I do not think it is a well founded complaint, that the same authority is not

given him in regard to those officials to be appointed under clause (d). But I have a good deal of difficulty in seeing where the outrage presents itself in the fact that we extend the right to the leader of the Opposition to nominate half of the gentlemen who are to do the counting. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Pugsley) has spoken of the minor and inferior officers and people of no importance at all in the conduct of this election. I respectfully beg to differ from him in that regard. I ask the House what criticism we should have been subjected to if, when we, dealing with a new class of officers-a class of officers that does not exist under the Dominion Election Act, a class of officers for whose services there is no occasion in a general election, a class of officers who are to be responsible for the proper counting and return of the ballots-we had not given the leader of the Opposition the right to have a say in the selection. That strikes me as a very important part of the work of an election. There was a very wise gentleman, who wrote a large number of articles replete with wisdom, and written in a most eloquent brogue, who put it forward as a suggestion for the settlement of the difficulties which eventuated in the Boer war that if he had been allowed to he could have settled the matter perfectly-that he would have been quite satisfied to allow them to give votes to whomsoever they chose provided only that they would allow him to count the ballots. I think that there is no operation of more importance than the counting of the ballots.
It is more important to get them in the bag in this case.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We will come to that in a moment. To represent it as an operation [DOT]of no importance, of so slight an importance that it is an outrage on the leader of the Opposition to give him the opportunity of *appointing one-half of the people who are going to do that counting and, furthermore, to provide that no counting shall be done without one officer of his nomination being present at it, is a statement that I frankly confess I am incapable-
The member for St. John will probably withdraw the word " outrage " if the minister will tell us he will accept the amendment.
Call it an insult.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am asked to agree to an amendment to clause (d) as a condition 
to my refraining from making any observations about the section that is objected to. I cannot quite grasp what the objection to clause (d) is. It has been offered to withdraw the word "outrage". If that word is withdrawn, then I would understand that the objection made to clause (d) is withdrawn, because thait is the only objection I *have heard. However, it is for the leader of the Opposition to determine what is the proper course for him to take in regard to clause (c). It was not inserted with any intention of offering offence and it is a matter of surprise to me that it should be suggested that there can be a word used to indicate that there is anything offensive in *it. As regards the amendment, I do not *know that it would be useful for me to go over what I said this afternoon. When we come to deal with this amendment we are dealing with a class of officers who have existed under the Elections Act so long as we have had elections; and the universal practice has been that the Government should appoint them andi be responsible for their appointment, as the Government must be responsible for the carrying on of the election. Now we are asked to abdicate that function simply because it is soldiers whose votes are going to be taken under the direction of each presiding officer; for it is not a question of the deputy presiding officer but of the presiding officer. It is soldiers' votes that are to be taken in France and England and the suggestion is that because that happens it necessarily follows that we ought to call m the Opposition to share with us the duty of appointing these public officers and, naturally, the responsibility for the carrying on of the election. I have not heard any *reason advanced that could not be equally applied to the appointment of returning officers in tlris country. I am not at all prepared to accept the argument that because a mah is appointed to a public office to do the business of the state, by the Government, that he is necessarily a partisan, and such a partisan as will abuse his position to give advantage to the party to which the Government which appointed him happens to belong. In all frankness, do we all stand here charging the returning officers in all the constituencies of Canada, ever since there has been a Dominion and we have had elections, with having been that kind of partisan and with having subjected the members of this House to injustice? I think the implication is most unfair and not justified by the facts or by experience. There may be cases

where a returning officer, because he was appointed by a certain government, or not so much because he was appointed as because he individually happened to be an unscrupulous partisan, has abused his position. But I have been through two elections and in each case the party to which I was opposed was in power; they appointed the returning officer and he appointed deputy returning officers, and I never had ground to complain against that gentleman;
I never saw that he did not perform his duties perfectly fairly and impartially from start to finish, and I am quite satisfied that hon. gentlemen from every other constituency can give the same testimony. I cannot subscribe to the doctrine that because a man is appointed to this important public office by the Government, that necessarily means that he is going to be a partisan of the type that will violate his oath and abuse his office for the purpose of favouring the party represented by the Government which appointed him. That is the one reason that is advanced. We have never heard this presiding officer mentioned to-day without the prefix " partisan. The prefix, of course, applies necessarily, if it applies to him, to every returning officer and every deputy returning officer who has acted in any election in this country, and to all of those who will adt in the election that is to come; and yet we have not had any suggestion that in this country the Government should abdicate this function and duty of appointing the returning officers. I can see no reason why we should depart, with regard to these precisely similar officers, from the rule which has been the custom for so long and that is still the law in this country.

In view of the minister's statement that the Government should not at all abdicate its exclusive right to conduct an election, why has he given to the leader of the Opposition the right to name one-half of these special returning officers?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
If the fault found with me is that I gave that right to the leader of the Opposition, then, of course, it is with some little surprise that I discover that fault is found, but to avoid criticism for having done that I would consent to withdraw the clause giving that power. If consistency is so precious a jewel that, rather than I should lose it, the hon. gentleman would prefer that I should not extend that power to the leader of the Opposition, I will be willing to withdraw that clause. I have said what I have to say on that clause, and
I have pointed out that the reason this .provision was made is that this is the first time that there has been occasion for the services of officers of this kind. We are dealing now with a very special office, one that has not existed in the past and an office the holders of which are to perform duties, in my opinion, of the very first importance. We are also providing for an operation where there will,be very material advantages to result from the fact that the same individual fills the public office and also acts, perfectly frankly and fairly, as the representative of his party to see that things .are done Tight. And that brings me to a moment's consideration of what is proposed here. With regard to counting officers and returning officers, they are to act in couples. This operation will be carried on by the two together; the one .and the same operation is participated in and controlled by the representatives of each parly. What is in the mind of the hon. gentleman with regard to presiding officers? One-half of them will be named by the leader of the Opposition and one-half will be named by the leader of the Government.
Those two presiding officers do not act together, and the reason put forward for requiring this is that the man named by the Government will necessarily be a partisan of the Government. It is not unfair, then, to conclude on the same reasoning, that the man named by the leader of the Opposition will be a partisan of the Opposition. With a nomination of that kind, we withdraw from the man who holds the position any idea that, whatever the complexion of the government that appointed him he is a representative of the whole state .and is charged with the duty of being faithful to the whole people. When you divide them up in this way, -and have one of them the nominee of the Opposition, and the other the nominee of the Government, it is notice to them that they are to be representatives of political parties, and what is going to happen?

Why did the minister appoint special returning officers, half of whom are to be nominated by the leader of the Opposition, to do the counting and recording? Ordinarily the counting is done by the returning officer.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
What was the purpose of this provision?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Ordinarily the counting is done by the returning officer. I should

like to ask the hon. gentleman from Halifax how he would suggest that, in the taking of the soldiers' votes, the presiding officer should count the ballots. The hon. member, when he suggests that, must certainly forget that the deputy presiding officer will be taking the votes of a group of soldiers.
No, that is not the point.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Then I would be glad to understand it.

I simply asked why in this Bill power is taken to permit the appointment on the recommendation of the leader of the Opposition of one-half of the special returning officers. I do not object to it. I think it should be there, and I do not agree with the hon. gentleman from St. John in that respect. But why give that power to the leader of the Opposition in that case, and not in the other case?

I wish to correct my hon. friend. I said exactly what the hon. gentleman says. I says it is an insult to the leader of the Opposition to have the provision in respect to the inferior officer and refuse it in respect to the important officer.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
May I take it that the clause is adopted? Here are hon. gentlemen vying with each other to say how perfectly satisfied they are that that should be done with reference to the returning officer. The hon. member for Halifax asks me why I did that. I must express my regret that I have such a marked incapacity for conveying my ideas. Whether the reason be sufficient or not, just a few moments ago I gave the reasons which led me to do that.
I will be glad to repeat them if it is necessary.
The hon. minister did it because he thought it was a fair thing to do, and would eliminate suspicion?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
Why not apply the same idea to clause (d)? '

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I did it because I
thought it was a fair thing to do, and because we were dealing with an entirely new phase, conferring functions upon this man to be carried out under conditions absolutely different from those under which the counting of ballots is ever done. I did not do it to avoid suspicion, I did it because I believed it to be fair and unobjectionable. If I had done it in the hope

of avoiding suspicion, I may say that I would have been grievously disappointed, because all I seem to have earned by it is a grave suspicion with regard to the presiding officer. This assortment and counting of ballots as proposed will very probably have to be done under conditions where there will be a number of acting returning officers and a number of clerks busy assorting ballots from numerous different constituencies and counting those ballots at the same time. If one sought to provide for representation of the party merely by scrutineers or agents, it might present very serious practical inconvenience to provide agents for both parties to watch the operations of these numerous groups of acting returning officers and their clerks and it seemed to me that there was a direct practical advantage in providing that the people doing the work should really fill the dual office of assorters or counters of ballots and of representatives of the party. I had a new function to confer; it was one, in my mind, of very great importance; and I thought that it would be, as the hon. gentleman says, a fair thing. Because I did that I am now asked to abdicate what has been the function of governments even since we have had elections with regard to an officer whose duties are on all fours with those of the ordinary returning officer-in fact not as important, because he has not to do with the official return with regard to the election. I am not prepared to accept the doctrine that this Government is incapable of appointing to a position of that kind any except a partisan, those capable of using the office for the purpose of fraud and of partisanship; men who will see to it that every deputy presiding officer they appoint shall be equally a partisan capable of violating his oath and using his office for the purpose of fraud. I am quite satisfied there is no foundation for the suspicion which I have aroused by my simple desire to guard this new and very peculiar office with what I am prepared to admit is a most extraordinary precaution. While I was not doing it to ward off suspicion, certainly it was one of the last things that I could have imagined would have brought upon me all this suspicion.
As regards the amendment, I certainly cannot, for the reasons I have given, accept the proposal, and I trust that members of the committee will agree with me that it is not a proposal which I can fairly be expected to accept.

I hope the minister will reconsider his position in respect to the amendment offered by the hon. member for St. John, and will yet accept it. It is a pity we should take up a whole hour getting nowhere, and having the whole issue befogged, when we might make progress by the minister accepting the amendment. I rise particularly to second his amendment. The conditions surrounding the taking of the military vote in Europe are in no respect similar to the conditions surrounding the polling of votes in ordinary elections. I make the suggestion to him in a friendly spirit that I do not think he gave the committee any reason to justify the position he took a moment ago in refusing to accept the amendment.
He has stated that the Government should not be expected to forego a function usually exercised by a government during election time. Quite true; but the premise is wrong; the conditions are dissimilar. In taking an election in Canada in ordinary times, it does not matter much who the returning officers or the deputy returning officers are. In the constituency of Halifax in the Dominion elections half the deputy returning officers are Conservatives and half Liberals. Although the returning officer in that constituency is a Liberal, he will likely be the returning officer during this election, notwithstanding the fact that the Conservative party is in power.

If there is no point of order before the Chair I am quite satisfied, but if there is a point of order I desire to speak to it, and to say that I am not satisfied to sit in this House and have the freedom of debate exercised by critics of this side of the House when we in turn are not expected to reply in kind. The events in connection with the voting in the province of British Columbia have no bearing upon any part of this Bill, yet a great part of the time of the House has been taken up to-day by one hon. gentleman after another in relating those occurrences. I wish to say on behalf of the province of British Columbia that that province had very little part in creating the occurrences which have been recited here. As to the recital itself, it is that of a partisan commission representing only one side of the issue before the electors, and representing the political faith of the government appointing it. I have not read their report, and all I have heard of it is what was read to the House to-day by the hon. member for Pictou.

But that had nothing to do with the taking, of the soldiers' votes on the political issue as to which, as explained oy the hon. member for Vancouver (Mr. Stevens) no fault has been found. What occurred was that when they came to the vote on prohibition, the prohibition party abandoned any attempt at scrutineering, and allowed the other party to complete the vote without any surveillance at all. Is it remarkable that frauds should occur under those circumstances?-circumstances which are not at all contemplated by this Act, and circumstances which have a parallel in the province of Quebec, where a vote was taken on the question of prohibition under precisely similar circumstances. I say this in justice to the province of British Columbia, where, with one solitary exception, we have been entirely free from political voting scandals.

If any further reason could possibly be needed in support of the amendment of my hon. friend from St. John, the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat has given it. He has given us an excellent illustration of what may happen in the taking of this vote. I had no idea that such a thing might be done when we were discussing this Bill on former occasions, but the hon. gentleman apparently knows what is intended to be done. He is, however, labouring under a difficulty; he expresses sympathy for the officers who will represent the right hon. leader of the Opposition. He need not worry about that, because I can assure him he will not be asked to be one of them. Nor do I think he need worry about the other officers who may be asked, because I have no doubt they will be just as capable of looking after themselves, and of fighting at the front, as my hon. friend. I would point out to the Minister of Justice that probably only a few presiding officers will be appointed under this Bill, and they will have the right to appoint deputies. For that reason, if for no other, I think an equal number could very well be appointed, and they could then consult together as to the appointment of their deputies, and I have n'ot the slightest doubt that they could easily agree upon the .appointment of deputies who would be practically non-partisan; and it is only to avoid partisanship that we want this done. The amendments to paragraphs (a), (b) and (c) seem to me to be perfectly all right. As to the minister's point, that the Government always appoints the deputy returning officers in
Canada, his comparison is not on all-fours with this case, because in Canada every candidate has a scrutineer to help him not only in the taking of the vote, but at the counting of the vote. If I may turn to section 8, subsection 3, I would point out that it says: "Where conditions make it reasonably possible the deputy presiding officer shall give public notice," etc. Subsection 5 says: "The deputy presiding officer may take ^uch vote otherwise than at a formally held poll." I think that if the minister would accept this amendment he would remove to a very great extent the faults we find in this Bill. I do not believe there are many, if any, hon. gentlemen on this side of the House who do not want to see the Bill go through as rapidly as possible, but at the same time they want to see it made as perfect as possible. This is a fact which cannot be controverted. The fact that under those conditions and at that time it was possible that a total disregard of the rules and laws which relate to proper voting should exist, is ample justification of the position taken by hon. gentlemen that under this Bill there should be no possibility of these things arising, and that we should place upon this vote such safeguards that everybody in the country should feel that the boys at the front were given a full and fair opportunity to express their views, and that their vote was honestly recorded. Hon. gentlemen have indulged in heroics on the question of who should have a vote under this Bill, but, if we send to the boys a Bill under which they are to voice their opinion, no matter what it may be, and that voice can be perverted by officials on whom there are not these ordinary checks which should be provided in cases of that kind, and if we are to have returning officers who are to be permitted to do what was done under the British Columbia Act, how are we oer-forming our duty to the boys at the front?

There were no

.resent any such imputation from the gentleman who has made them. Loyalty is not a mere matter of lip-service. pretend that is the custom in Nova Scotia?

That is the practice in certain counties in Nova Scotia.
