I would scarcely have thought the language was intended to mean the Clerk of the Crown must go there personally, I think I have examined other parts of the Bill sufficiently to enable me to state that there is no provision for keeping count of the ballots which are printed.

They should be official ballots. As I understand, the officer in England can have as many (ballots struck off as he pleases. There is no limitation. I think it is only a reasonable precaution that there should he a certain number of official ballots, and all the ballots which are handed to the presiding officers should be accounted for. There would be a certain number used, so many ballots returned, and so many ballots spoiled. Any of those official ballots which have not been used should be returned to the proper officers at Ottawa. There is no provision in regard to that. This measure only provides for the commanding officer making returns of ballots, but there is no cheek on the ballot papers which are issued by the officer in London, or by the officer, in Ottawa. It seems to me there should be a careful check upon those ballot papers, so that the number of ballots left on hand would be known, and would be a safeguard against duplication of ballots and against ballots being printed by others than those who are officially authorized to print them.
I think my hon. friend will find that his objection is met in section 13.
Will the Minister of Justice explain what countries are included in the designation: "In any other place without Canada but in North America"?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That would cover the entire continent with the exception of Canada.
What are the places included?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There are soldiers in Bermuda; some of our boys are serving in the patrol motor boat service, the headquarters of which are at Trinidad, and there are soldiers at St. Lucia. This provision applies only [DOT] to those places where commanding officers are in charge of troops. Under the last Act we would have been subject to embarrassment because we mentioned Bermuda specifically, and it afterwards happened that some of our soldiers -not a very large number, it is true-were at St. Lucia.
Is St. Lucia in North America?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I understand it to be. It is not on the mainland, of course, but I understand that the term "North America" would include the adjacent islands.
St. Lucia is not adjacent to the continent.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is in North America to the same extent that Great Britain is in Europe. Any geography would include these islands in North America.
There were only 15 or 20 men in St. Lucia.

The member for North
Simcoe (Mr. Currie) said that section 13 would cover the point that I made with (reference to the ballots. I have read the ^section, and I find that my hon. friend is (entirely mistaken. It relates to a different .matter altogether.

The section reads:
Notwithstanding anything contained in Part III, every returning officer appointed and acting under that Part in respect ol an electoral district wherein a poll is held, as soon as ho has made the final addition of the votes polled pursuant to that Part, shall, without dec)ar->
ing any candidate elected and without making the return required by section two hundred and eleven of that Part, make, sign and seal a certificate stating the number of votes given for each candidate, as determined by such final addition, and the report required by section two hundred and thirteen of Part Illy and transmit to the general returning officer the writ of election together with such certifi-. cate and report, the stamp furnished him for stamping the ballot papers, and all the ballot papers, including those unused, the original statements of the several deputy returning officers, the lists of voters, the poll books used in the several polling divisions, and all other lists and documents furnished for the election; or which have been transmitted to him by the deputy returning officers.
The Clerk of the Crown in Chancery sends a certain number of ballots to the returning officer, as in an ordinary election, and ultimately gets them back.

My hon. friend will
pardon me; section 13 deals entirely with ian election held under part 3, which is a provision of the Dominion Elections Act.
All the Dominion Elections Act applies to this. Where this Act does not apply, the other does.

This section provides, in the form of the schedule, the kind of ballot to be used in this section. The ballot makes provision for the military elector casting a vote for the Government, for the Opposition or for an independent candidate. This is a designation of party upon the ballot which has never existed in any British country in theory or in practice. On that ground I must express regret that the minister has seen fit to adopt that form of ballot. Things may happen before the next election takes place which would make it difficult to determine the exact position

of some candidates in the party 10 p.m. sense. The member for Annapolis (Mr. Davidson) expressed his hope for the organization of a union Government. If that hope should be fulfilled, there would be a temporary obliteration of party lines in this country, at least to some extent. It would not be binding, however, upon the member for North Sim-coe (Mr. Currie) or upon any other person. The member for St. Antoine (Sir Herbert Ames) says that even in that event there would be an Opposition. Well, if a union Government were organized it would take some time for an Opposition to evolve. They might not have sufficient time prior to polling day to become a political organization in the sense in which the Liberal party to-day is an Opposition party. Many other things might happen to make a ballot of this kind impracticable and unfair. My view is that the ballot should contain the name of the candidates; no matter what happens, that is the fair thing. It is fair to everybody. The hon. member for St. Antoine shakes his head. What is his objection?

If you will look through the service roll of any battalion overseas, you will find the battalion is made up of men from probably fifty different points in Canada. If that battalion is at a certain point in France near the front, do you mean, to tell me that you can supply the men with a complete set of ballots for every candidate in Canada?

Is that the only objection?
! Sir HERBERT AMES: That is one which it seems to me is sufficient in itself.

Let us suppose there are three candidates, Smith, Jones and Brown, in a particular constituency. Does the hon. member suggest that we should also print on the ballot paper that Smith was for the Government, Jones for the Opposition, and Brown independent?
I did not intend any party designation of candidates whatever.
Then you would be up against a very serious difficulty, because the soldier would in many cases not know whether Brown or Smith was for or against the Government, and he would have to vote blind.

That is true to some extent, but even then it would be a more intelligent vote than where the ballots are simply marked for the Government or for the Opposition, particularly in cases where the man is not able to indicate an electoral district, when the Prime Minister or the leader of the Opposition really names the candidates voted for.

Let us suppose there are four hundred candidates. Now there might be four or five hundred men in a battalion who would wish to vote in some electoral district. In order to insure there being a sufficient number of ballot papers you would have to put two hundred thousand papers, -four hundred multiplied by at least five hundred-in the hands of each deputy returning officer. I want to see the soldiers vote properly, and if the hon. member can suggest any better method I should be willing to support him.

My hon. friend has suggested a difficulty, but I do not think the difficulty 'is insuperable. In many cases you will find several battalions belonging to one province close together, and then there would be very little difficulty such as my hon. friend suggests. Take my own case, for instance, as an illustration of how this proposal might work a hardship. The hon. member for New

Westminster said a few moments ago that conscription would be the issue with the military elector. Assume that I am a candidate in the next election, which is possible. In my constituency there will he four candidates. The Prime Minister will be one, in support of the Conscription Bill.
I also supported the Bill. Now in that case it would be almost impossible for any military elector from the constituency of Halifax to vote, if the only consideration was the attitude of the Prime Minister and myself upon the Conscription Bill, and that attitude were judged merely by the vote in the House. That one illustration alone raises a very difficult question, and I submit that this form of ballot hardly meets the situation. In the province of New Brunswick they have a form of ballot which perhaps might be used here. The official envelope is provided by the Government, and the ballot is enclosed in it after being marked by the elector. The candidates in a provincial election in New Brunswick prepare their own ballot, having tneir own ' names printed on them if they like, or they can supply the voter with a blank piece of paper and he can write on it the name of the candidate for whom he desires to vote. The protection is in the envelope. The procedure in New Brunswick might possibly be useful in considering this matter. I do not like the idea of giving statutory recognition of party in a ballot. We have never done it in this country, nor has it been done in any other part of the British Empire. In theory there is no such thing as party in our constitution. It may be true, as the hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. Currie) suggests, that there will be difficulty in the way of printing the names of the candidates. I admit that it may be difficult to meet some of the objections which could be raised against my own suggestion, but I think upon the whole it will be less objectionable than that proposed in the ballot form in the schedule. I do not think there is any difficulty in having the ballot bearing the names of the candidates nominated in each constituency put before the military electors. By the use of the cable the names of these candidates could be in Great Britain and in Europe 25 or 27 days before polling day; then in all the camps, the hospitals and other places where our forces are assembled, the names of the different candidates in each constituency can be printed in the usual manner, and within a period of two or three weeks the military electors will become acquainted with the name of each candidate. In the
British Columbia elections there was a polling held at Halifax. There was an official ballot, but the names of the candidates were not printed upon it. I had something to do with that polling on behalf of the Lib ral candidates in British Columbia. The Government did not even furnish the men with the names of the candidates on either side. Those names were supplied to the voters at Halifax by friends of both parties in British Columbia. I remember in the city of Vancouver there was quite a number of candidates on both sides, and it was found that most of the soldiers voting knew hardly any of them. A good many of the soldiers knew Mr. Bowser's name, because he had been so long before the public of British Columbia, but it was almost the only name upon the ballot that was known to the soldier voters who had to vote in the city of Vancouver. If you have the ballot printed with the name of the candidate upon it, and have the usual notices posted at the camps, gradually the electors will become acquainted with the names of the candidates in the district which they are likely to designate as their electoral district. I submit that this form of ballot should be changed, and that we should endeavour to have the names of the candidates printed on the ballot.

I listened with some amusement to the hon. member for Halifax working out in his own mind an absolutely unworkable scheme. There is no question about it that a ballot could not be prepared or used in the manner indicated toy my hon. friend, particularly in Prance. There is with each battalion on an average of about one thousand men. Even presuming that the majority of these men are from one constituency, yet a deputy presiding officer would have to carry anywhere from 200,000 to 400,000 ballots in order to be sure he would have a ballot available for a man from any constituency. Many battalions in Canada went over in the first place from one constituency. These battalions have been broken up and the men scattered around among other battalions from the Atlantic to the Pacific. Men have been wounded, have gone back to England, and when they recovered and were sent hack to France again they did not return to their original battalions. Then we have corps like the engineers, raised from the Atlantic to the Pacific. You will find in one small company of engineers, consisting of 700 or 800 men, men from almost every constituency in the country.

Another consideration is this-as has been pointed out by the hon. gentleman himself -the men would be unacquainted with a great many of the candidates. There is also another point. The men at the front do not know, in many cases, what constituency they belong to. We had a revision of the constituencies in this country, and there are men over there now who have no idea as to what constituency they belong to. It is absolutely necessary to get the information from the man himself in some way, perhaps not exactly in the form we have it on the back of this ballot, but the information must be obtained from the man as to the locality from which he comes, so that his vote may be properly allocated to that constituency. The junior member for Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) says they will have 27 days to prepare those papers and the ballots, but he must remember that part of those 27 days will be taken up by the voting. Some of the men must vote before the expiration of the last week. Some of the men must vote before they go to the trenches, 'and others after they come out.
Mr. C. A. WILSOij7:	The same thing
happens here. There are many people who cannot vote here.
That is no reason why the soldiers should not vote. We want to make this Act so that the soldier can vote.

I would like to draw atr tention to the fact that there is a great likelihood of spoiled ballots because of writing in the name. In the province of New Brunswick we have a ballot on which either the names are printed or the voter may write in the name of the candidate for whom he wishes to vote. Because of this conflict between the local ballot and the federal ballot, a great many ballots are spoiled.
It is not am unusual occurrence to. find a cross prat in front of some of the names, thus spoiling the ballot. One danger, I think, would be to allow the voter to write the name of the candidate he wishes to vote foT, unless he had something to guide him. He would likely think that was sufficient, whereas, as I understand it, the ballot would be spoiled unless there was a cross after the name.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Not in this proposed
ballot. If the voter simply writes in the space " I vote for Mr. Loggie" that will be a vote for my hon. friend, without any cross, or anything being added to it.
But, if in addition to that he puts a cross at the end of it, would that spoil the ballot?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No.

That covcts the difficulty I had in mind on that score. Another question which presented itself to my mind was the question of the independent candidate. I see that is qualified under another section, rather along the lines that there should not' be more than three condidates, namely, a Government candidate, an Opposition candidate, and an Independent candidate. I can conceive of cases where there might possibly be two Independent candidates.

I think there are five
in one Ontario constituency now.
There may be an Independent Liberal candidate.
Impossible!

Or there might be an Independent Conservative candidate. I simply draw the attention of the minister to the ballot in New Brunswick, where voting in local elections was entirely different from that in federal elections, and we found a great many ballots spoiled because of that. It is very desirable that it should toe made clear to the voters, so that the same thing would not happen in this case.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I wdsh to say a word in reference to the remarks of the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean). In the first place the hon. member observed that such a form of ballot had never been used in any British country. I hold in my hand the form of ballot used in the Australian election that is on all fours with ours.
I know, but I said that no such ballot had been used in [DOT] ordinary times.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Well, we are in extraordinary times. It seems to me that'the ballot we propose has all the advantages which the hon. gentleman was claiming for the ordinary ballot, and has in addition the advantage of enabling men, of whom there may be many, who do not know the candidates, and who do not connect them either with the Government or the Opposition, to express their opinion whether for the Government or for the Opposition, while at the same time it does not take away from them the privilege of voting for individual candidates if they desire to do so. When we come to the other provisions of the Bill

my hon. friend will find that there is a special provision for taking all the steps that we could think of to enable the soldier to become aware of who the candidates are. If we are successful in conveying that information to the soldier, and as a result of that information he wishes to vote for an individual candidate of whom he knows, he can do it with this ballot.
Does not that only apply to the case of Bermuda and other places outside of Canada but in North America?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No, we have made provision for the sending of information with regard to the nomination of candidates to the other side as well as to Bermuda and other places, and we have also provided that the special officers over there shall take means of spreading this information. While we have tried to take every step possible to get the information to the soldier, we cannot, of course, count that every soldier will get the information, nor even that, if every soldier gets the information that John Jones and Peter Brown are nominated in his constituency, he will know what John Jones and Peter Brown represent. To the extent that we get the information to the man, if he had the ballot in the form which the hon. member for Halifax suggests, he would be in a position to use it. Then we hand him a ballot by which he can do identically the same thing, that is, write in the name of the man for whom he wants to vote. If he should happen not to have that information, then we present him with a ballot which leaves him in a position to vote for his,preference for the Government candidate, or the Opposition candidate, or the Independent candidate. By handing out this ballot we do not deprive a man who is in a position to do it by reason of the knowledge which he possesses of the opportunity of voting for the individual candidate. But we make it possible for every man to exercise his franchise to the extent of voting for the Government, or the Opposition, or the Independent candidate. Then, as ha6 been pointed out by my hon. friend from Fron-tenac (Mr. Edwards), if a man who gets a ballot with nothing on it but the names of the candidates, may or may not know what it is that these men stand for, he may or may not know anything about them and he may have no personal preference in regard to them. That man with the ballot advocated by the hon, member for Halifax would be called upon to vote in the
dark, whereas with the ballot we offer him, if his reasons are personal, then he may vote for the candidate whom he favours.
If his reasons are not personal, and he desires to support the Government, or the Opposition, or an Independent representative, he still has an opportunity of recording his vote in accordance with his own opinion. We take nothing from the man by giving him this ballot instead of giving him the ordinary printed ballot, but we do afford an opportunity to him, should he be in a position where the ordinary ballot would not be useful to him, to still record his vote in the manner we have provided for. What has been stated by hon. gentlemen who speak with practical experience of conditions over on the other side is conclusive as to the feasibility of carrying out the other plan. In the preparation of the Bill we gave serious thought to the question whether four weeks would be long enough to afford an opportunity to gather in the votes, and if we have to lose eight or ten days in getting these distributed to the proper officers, it will take a very long time. On the other hand, as has been pointed out, if the presiding officer has to go out equipped to take the votes in any possible constituency he will have to carry a tremendous number of ballots. Then, if there were not this practical objection, what I said at the outset is a conclusive proof that a man loses no advantage by this system of ballots. If he is in the possession of knowledge that enables him to vote for an individual candidate, he can do it, and if he is not in that position he may still vote by reason of the form of this ballot.

This form ought to have the word "candidate" after the words "Government" and "Opposition." "I vote for the Government" is rather a meaningless phrase. We should put in "I vote for the Government candidate" or "I vote for the Opposition candidate."

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We might add the word "candidate."
You have at the bottom this form of ballot: "I vote for the Independent candidate."

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, because we could hardly describe the Independent candidate without using the words "Independent candidate." The Australian ballot says "Ministerial" and "Opposition" and the voter records his vote by putting a cross opposite the word "Ministerial" or "Opposition."
Or writing in the name of any other person.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Or writing in the name of any other person. The printing of the additional word "candidate" will involve the use of the word "candidate" or "candidates." I do not see what is gained by that additional printing because we have a provision in the Act for determining to whom the votes that are given for the Government and for the Opposition shall be applied. We get no further by the use of the word "candidate" being printed on the ballot inasmuch as the provision of the Act is that a ballot marked "I vote for the Government" is counted for the Government candidate or candidates and a ballot marked "I vote for the Opposition" is counted for the Opposition candidate or candidates.

Supposing there are more than two candidates in the field; that in certain constituencies there are four candidates, two to be elected. A man wants to vote for one of those who is a Government candidate and for another who is an Opposition candidate. Can he mark his ballot as voting for the Government and also mark it as voting for the Opposition, or write in the name of any other man? How is he to record his vote?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Such a man would know the candidates and would be able to write in the names of those for whom he wished to vote.
In the Australian ballot that is all provided for; the number of candidates is mentioned and there is a space for the two names where there are more than two candidates.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There is plenty of space to write in two names on our ballots.
Suppose a man voting for Halifax marked his ballot "I vote for Maclean," and on the same ballot voted for the Government candidate, would such a ballot be counted or be defective?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Of course there may be combinations of circumstances where the man will not be able to record his vote just as he wishes, but I should like to dispose of one thing at a time. I should be disposed to believe that if there was a constituency where a man was entitled to two distinct votes there would be no difficulty in taking his vote.

I had the city of Halifax in mind and there might be two Govern-
TMr. Doherty.!
ment candidates. How would he indicate the Government candidate for whom he wished to vote?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: He would write in the name of the Government candidate for whom he wished to vote. I cannot conceive of a man having a personal preference for people whose names he does not know.
\\U11 these instructions be circulated among the soldiers?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, instructions similar to those for elections generally.

Will the minister say definitely whether the ordinary Elections Act applies to the taking of this vote? There are many precautions in reference to the ballot paper itself in the General Elections Act, such as paper of a prescribed weight, which is furnished by the King's Printer, and then the man who prints the vote fyles an affidavit describing the paper and giving the number of ballots supplied, and stating that no other ballot papers have been supplied by him to any one else. These are very important and necessary precautions.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not think these provisions apply, and I do not think it would be possible to make them apply. The King's Printer could not furnish the paper on which ballots are to be printed on the other side of the ocean, partly owing to the difficulty of securing transportation, and partly owing to the danger of the ballots being lost in transit. The ballots are to be provided by the acting clerk of the Crown in Chancery in England. The other provisions that have to do with the printing of the ballot in the different constituencies by the returning officers could not be made applicable to the ballots that are to be printed for the use of 400,000 or 500,000 electors overseas.
I think that we can trust the acting Clerk of the Crown in Chancery to take such precautions as may be possible to control the ballots, but under the system provided here it would not be a great evil if some ballots that were not originally printed got into circulation. No ballot will be counted in this election unless it reaches the commissioner's office in France, or the commissioner's office in London, enclosed in a properly sealed up receptacle or box-the word " bag " makes some people nervous, so I would not like to mention it-and marked on the outside as military votes, containing in the interior all the papers

used in the election, with the num'ber of envelopes contained in it set forth and signed and certified by the military officer who is, at the same tune, the deputy presiding officer, and every one of these ballots in an envelope containing the description of the man that voted. Really I do not think there is any great danger to he apprehended, supposing somebody managed to get hold of the ballots in the form provided here. The precautions that are both possible and desirable, when you are dealing with the printing of ballots which are being printed in the constituencies all over Canada, not under one general control or direction, but by different printers scattered all over the country, may have their reason for existence, and may be useful, and, perhaps, even necessary, tout I do not think they are practicable in an election of this kind, and I do not think there is any serious danger to be apprehended by reason of the fact that they are not to be used under this Bill. We have to depart from some things that may be very useful in their way, if we are going to get the soldiers' vote. There is no substantial danger attendant upon the fact that the ballots are not being printed in that way. This question of precautions with regard to ballots was very thoroughly threshed out at the time we passed the Act of 1915, and it was not then found necessary to surround the printing of those ballots with all the formalities that are indicated in that section, and the present section reproduced that law with the distinction that I have pointed out, that as regards the overseas vote, the ballots shall not be sent from here by the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery, but shall be provided over there by the assistant Clerk of the Crown in Chancery.
I suppose that by the regulations which are provided for in the Act the officers on the other side will have ballot papers about -the same as we have them here?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, by the regulation we will try to make provision for every detail we can properly control to make the ballot paper as effective a thing as it can be made. Those regulations will all be published, and everybody will know what they are.

I think it would be preferable to make a change in the arrangement of the order on the ballot. The great bulk of the voters will vote either for the Government or for the Opposition.
The voters will commence at the top, and read down, and I think it would lead to confusion if the first thing they see is a blank for an individual. They would be very likely, if they knew his special candidate, to write his name in there, and then go further down and mark the ballot for the Government or the Opposition. The proper way would be to have first, Government, then Opposition and then Independent candidate, and if a voter does not vote for one of the three, he comes to the foot of the ballot, and writes in the name of the candidate. The number who write in the name will be small, because 95 per cent will vote for Government, Opposition or Independent candidate. I think there would be less likelihood of mistakes, if the ballots were prepared in that way. The Australian ballot reads in this way: first Government, then Opposition, and at the foot there is a line, and if you do not wish to vote for the Ministerial or Opposition candidate, you can write on the line the name of the man you want to vote for.

I think the Australian ballot is an improvement on the ballot in the draft Bill. The point I wished to make was not that I anticipated any trouble from the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery m England, but the difficulty to my mind is in regard to the printer. If some London printer prints those ballots, there can be no reason why the same rule should not apply to that printer as applies to the Canadian printer. All he has to do is to make a short affidavit, stating the number of ballots he has printed, and that he has not printed any ballots for any one except the Clerk of tire Crown in Chancery or the officer to whom they are to be delivered. That is a proper precaution to be taken, and there is no difficulty in the way of taking it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I shall look into the
question. If that is applicable it will be made to apply, but as I pointed out, it is a provision about the printing of ballots which is being done for returning officers scattered all over the country. There may be necessity for a greater minutial of detailed instructions to those gentlemen, as to what they are to do, than is perhaps necessary when we are dealing with the printing operations which are going to be entrusted to the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery to look after, and if I could really see the substantial danger to be apprehended because the printer did not make the affidavit that he did not give some of

these ballots to somebody else, I would be glad to make that provision.

He might print too
many.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Supposing the awful
thing happened, and he printed too many, what harm would be done?

I will tell the hon. gentleman in a minute. It is a great advantage to a man who is intending to be fraudulent in an election to have possession of ballots, because he can distribute them to voters, and can mark them, and when the voter goes into the compartment he has a marked ballot in his pocket; he can change it for the ballot handed him, and all kinds of fraud can be performed by having a supply of printed ballots. The minister does not require me to tell him that, because it is one of the difficulties we meet in conducting an election. This precaution in regard to the printer was taken to avoid anything of that kind. It is a proper precaution, and I think the minister ought to adopt it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Whether it may be better or worse, the hon. gentleman is talking of a system which is not the system under this part of the Act. Under this section of the Act, as was the case under the Soldiers' Vote Act which is now in force, the provision for protection against that sort of thing is that the elector has to mark his ballot, not in a secret compartment, but where the presiding officer can see that the voter is marking the paper he gave him, but not seeing how he is marking it. This section is already the law, and when we come to deal with it, if we have to go over it again, I shall be glad to explain why it is necessary.
If we try to put minute details in an Act of this kind we may defeat our purpose, because under conditions that exist on-the other side it may not be possible to meet some of the detail that we have insisted upon. We asked the officer who had been, connected with the framing of the Act in Australia for advice as to how to make this Act effective. He made certain suggestions, but the thing that he insisted upon chiefly was that the law be not made rigid. He said: You have to make it as elastic as possible, consistently with the taking of the necessary precautions. If I thought that there was any substantial danger I might be disposed to make provision for the submission of an affidavit in the matter, but that does not strike me as being necessary.

The Minister of Justice seems to have such a clear grasp of the conditions of this Bill that I rise with a good deal of diffidence even to offer a suggestion. I notice that in this ballot there are columns 1, 2, 3 and 4, and that No. 4 contains the words: "I vote for the independent candidate." But there may be three or four independent candidates. There might be a Socialist candidate, a candidate representing the grain growers, or a candidate representing the labour interests. The Australian ballot has the clause: "I vote for the independent candidate whose name is written below." In some of the large centres'-Montreal, 'Toronto or Hamilton, and other cities-there might be three or four independent candidates. It seems to me that the Bill is incomplete in not providing that the name of the particular candidate may be indicated.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The Australian ballot could be utilized only in the way indicated if the voter knew the name of the independent candidate whom he wanted to vote for. Under our ballot, if he knows the name of the candidate for whom he wishes to vote, he has only to write the name in. According to the Australian plan the voter states two things: first, that he wants to vote for the independent candidate, and, second, that he wants to vote for John Smith. Under our legislatiqn, he will simply say: I want to vote for John Smith -and the result will be absolutely the same in either case. There may be difficulty if you have two or three independent candidates and the voter does not know whom to vote for, but when he knows the name, there will be no difficulty under our ballot.
I confess that I do not quite know how we can provide the means by which a man can vote, no matter what may be his degree of ignorance in regard to the conditions prevailing. The best we can do is to provide the means for the men to vote under circumstances which may reason-11 p.m. ably arise. There may be exceptional instances in which a man, by reason of his lack of knowledge or the lack of completeness of this ballot form, will not be able to find a method of expressing exactly what he wants. I think, however, that we get as near exactitude as we can get-certainly as near as the Australian ballot does get in this particular.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I shall be glad to ask the Minister of Militia if he can procure the information suggested. I think there is a great deal of force in what the hon. member has said as regards the order of the spaces, notwithstanding the suggestion of the hon. member for St. Antoine. With all the means that we are taking to circulate the information as to names, I would rather anticipate that the great bulk of these ballots will be marked by name, because if hon. gentlemen will look at the next section they will see that we have inserted a special provision that the names, addresses and descriptions of the several candidates who have been nominated shall be sent by the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery to every officer in command of Canadian troops in Bermuda, and to every presiding officer appointed to arrange for the holding of polls within Canada, and the Assistant Clerk of the Crown in Chancery transmits the information to all presiding officers of whose appointment he has been notified. We have not specified all the details of what these officers will do. It seemed to us that would be a more proper matter for regulations or for the instructions which it is provided are to be sent out.

I think every hon. gentleman who knows anything about mili-

tary matters will agree with me that it will be perfectly feasible and of great advantage to have all this information posted up on the battalion board, and I think we ought to have a provision to that effect in the Bill, rather than leave it to the instructions.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: When we come to the next section I would have no objection to providing that the presiding officers, when they receive the information, shall post it up in such manner as shall be' indicated. I should he glad to meet my hon. friend's .suggestion as to identifying the ballot if we could do that without creating too much red tape, but I think a moment's reflection will show that it is no small undertaking to impose on the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery the obligation of separating 500,000 distinct ballots, and affixing a stamp on each one of them.
There are hot that many Canadians on the other side.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There are 350,000 then.
Not on the other side. My hon. friend has not been following the figures.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman object to 250,000?	,
You are doing better.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It would be quite an undertaking for the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery to sit down and put on the ballots an identification mark that would be of any value. Would it be desirable, if it should happen that two ballots got stuck together, and one went unstamped, and was handed out to a soldier that his ballot should be rejected? While taking all reasonable precautions, I do not want to do anything that would involve the risk of a man losing his vote through non-compliance with a formality of this kind.

The votes of the men in camp in England could be taken just as easily as if they were in Canada. You have so many battalions in a camp, and all you have to do is to open your poll, and the vote can be taken just as easily as at home. There will be no trouble whatever at the camps in England, and there ought to be none in France, except in the case of the men in the front line trenches.

I would like to ask the minister what would be the effect if the name of a candidate were written on a ballot and a cross were marked opposite a

square which was inconsistent with the political affiliation of that candidate? For instance, if it so happened that the name of the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) was written in square No. 1 of the ballot, and a cross was marked in square No. 3, would that destroy the ballot?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think the hon. member for Frontenac might be combined with an independent candidate. I have some evidence of his qualifications in that regard, but I dare say he would not link up with the Opposition. At first glance I should think we would be face to face with a ballot in which a man had voted for both sides, if he had voted for the hon. member for Frontenac, and likewise voted for the Opposition.
Would it not mean that he was voting for the hon. member for Frontenac to go into Opposition?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Under the circumstances I do not see that we could treat it as otherwise than a vote for both sides, and it would not count. At the same time, I should imagine the predominant intention was to vote for the man whose name was indicated.

That was the point I intended to raise, and that was why I asked the Minister of Justice what his interpretation would be. It seems to me if the name of a candidate is written on the ballot, it clearly shows the intention of the voter to vote for that individual, and I think the vote should be counted for him, regardless as to whether or not there may be any inconsistency in the voter having placed a cross in any of the other squares. The object of the scheme is to secure the registration of the voter's intention, and if he names a man the vote should go to that man, regardless of what the voter may think the political affiliation of the candidate is.

In the case where there is only one man to be elected for a constituency, I should think that even although the elector voted for a man by name, and then also put his mark in the square for "Government" or "Opposition" if the leader of the Opposition was of the opinion that the man so named was the Opposition candidate the ballot should not be rejected, because there was a clear intention to vote for that man. A greater difficulty might arise in the case of a constituency where there are two members to

be elected. Suppose that in such a case the man wanted to vote for two members and put the name of one and then put a cross. Take St. John, for instance. Supposing the man wanted to vote for Mr. Hazen and myself. Suppose he wrote the name of Mr. Hazen and then put a cross in the space for the Opposition. In that case, could the two votes be counted? Suppose he put a cross in both squares, thus marking his ballot three times, would that spoil his ballot?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I would not be disposed to think that would spoil his ballot. For instance, a man who says "I vote for the Government" and then marks in "I vote for Mr. Hazen," assuming Mr. Hazen is the Government candidate, I think that man is simply saying the same thing twice, and I do not see any reason why his vote should not be counted.

Even if he wanted to
vote for me also?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If he ako says he votes for the Opposition, the difficulty that would arise would be to say which of the two Opposition candidates the vote ought to go to. Supposing the voter says "I vote for Mr. Hazen," and also marks a cross in the Opposition square. The man has a right to register two votes on that ballot, because there are two members to be elected. I should say if he says "I vote for Mr. Hazen" that vote should be counted for Mr. Hazen. If he says "I vote for the Opposition" that ought to be a good vote for the Opposition, because the elector is entitled to two votes. The difficulty that would arise, as was suggested a while ago, is for which of the two Opposition candidates could you count that vote?
I think you would have to reject the ballot in that c se.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not see why you should reject the ballot, for the voter had expressed a perfectly clear intention. Supposing he said "I vote for Mr. Pugsley" and he also marked a cross opposite "Government," I would not think it fair that my hon. friend should be deprived of the vote clearly expressed in his favour because of the fact that the other vote is not sufficiently clearly expressed to give it to somebody. That man has exercised one of the two votes in a perfectly unmistakable way. I do not think we should nullify that vote because unfortunately he used his other vote in such a way that we could not ascertain who it should go to.

Must it not be clear
from the ballot which two candidates he wanted to vote for? Say he wanted to vote for me, in the case you put, and that it was uncertain whether he wanted to vote for Mr. Hazen or for Mr. Hazen's colleague. Under this Bill I think the whole ballot would have to be rejected.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think perhaps we
might leave that for the courts to decide. The principle is that we should, so far as the intention is clearly ascertainable on the face of the ballot, but is not so expressed as to involve identification, give effect to that intention, and I think we should count that ballot.
There are five constituencies where that very thing may occur.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There is a special section under which the consideration of these questions may properly aTise. I refer to the section covering the method in which the ballots will be dealt with. We will have to consider the whole question when we take up that section. I think we should adopt any method that can be found to give effect to the intention of the voter.

I would like to add a
word to what has been said by the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle) in regard to the case of a voter who has plainly written the name of the candidate in space No. 1. Assuming he wrote the name of the Minister of Justice there.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: He could not do much better than that.

Probably so. In some
regards, I think the hon. gentleman is quite right. Having done that, there is a specific act on the part of that voter who has perhaps voted for the candidate for non-political reasons, or out of friendship, or through acquaintanceship. Then through confusion of the ballot, or perhaps by inadvertence, he puts a cross in the " Opposition " square. Surely it could not be contended that that would be a spoiled ballot? There can be, no plainer act done by the voter than to write the name in full of the candidate for whom he wishes to vote. It ought to be incumbent upon the minister to make that clear. The hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) has a lot of friends, some of them Tories, who vote for him. It would be a pity if such a mistake should be made by the voter. I would ask the minister to say that it would be an injustice to declare that a ballot shall be spoiled

where the voter writes the name of the candidate for whom he wishes to vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am inclined to think that it would be justifiable to accept the writing of the name as overriding the cross that would be put opposite the printed word "Opposition." I have made a note of it because we could only deal with it by way of an amendment to a section which comes later on and which describes how the ballots are to be counted. That would be the proper place to insert a provision to carry out what seems to me to be a pretty generally accepted view.
I suppose that if we allowed this section to pass it would not be understood that we would be at all committed to the form of ballot but that we could come back to it?,

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I would be open to any suggestion as to the form of ballot. I was quite impressed with the desirability of carrying out the suggestion of the hon. member for Pictou that we should add a space for a labour candidate.
If the minister would agree that we would be enabled to go back to it we might allow it to pass. But, we are not over all the difficulties yet.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I will make no difficulty about going back to the ballot if there is any suggestion to be made.

My hon. friend from Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) made a suggestion that might be applicable to this section and I think the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle) raised a very important point. If we would consent to this section being passed and then adjourn, the minister has assured us that he will have no objection to our going back or to making any suggestions concerning it. The real pith of the discussion is as to the form of the ballot which we have been discussing. Will that be satisfactory?	[DOT]
On the understanding that if we find that we have to move an amendment we will be able to do it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I shall not make any objection, if we cannot come to any agreement, to another amendment being suggested as long as the language is not too strong.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
Progress reported.
On montion of Hon. Mr. Doherty, the House adjourned at 11.35 p.m.
Wednesday, August 22, 1917.
